enrichment.short_title: Algerian asylum appeal: past detention and future Article 3 risk
key_facts: The appellant, a Berber Algerian citizen, arrived in the UK in February 1998 after military service and civilian work in Algiers.
He was detained and roughly treated on two occasions in 1995 and 1996 during generalised terrorist investigations, then released without charge and required to report fortnightly.
The adjudicator and IAT accepted past ill-treatment crossed the Article 3 threshold but found no real risk of repetition on return.
The appellant argued Demirkaya required inference of future risk from past persecution absent significant change of circumstances.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal to the Court of Appeal on a point of law from the Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissal of asylum and human rights appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the IAT lawfully concluded that despite past Article 3 ill-treatment there was no real risk of persecution or Article 3 harm if the appellant were returned to Algeria.
enrichment.ratio: Past persecution or Article 3 ill-treatment is probative of future risk but does not automatically establish a well-founded fear; the decision-maker must consider all relevant circumstances, including release without charge, lack of current interest by the authorities, and the appellant's ability to live openly in Algiers for months after ceasing to report; Demirkaya does not create an irrebuttable presumption from historic ill-treatment.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred in law by failing to treat past Article 3 ill-treatment as determinative of future risk
Proper application of Demirkaya v SSHD to Algerian detention history
Whether breach of reporting requirements created a real risk on return
Scope of appellate intervention in asylum cases where Article 3 is engaged
linked_authorities: Demirkaya v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1999] INLR 441
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Turgut [2001] 1 All ER 719
Adan v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1999] 1 AC 293

enrichment.short_title: Unduly lenient sentences for father and son aggravated burglary
key_facts: Thomas Eamon Barrow and his 17-year-old son Daniel attacked a man at his home at about 5.30 a.m. with a baseball bat, kicks and punches after a domestic grievance.
The victim suffered a smashed and dislocated nose requiring surgery and was forced to move home after 40 years in the property.
At Derby Crown Court the father received four years' imprisonment and the son two years' YOI detention, plus five-year ASBOs.
The Attorney General referred the sentences as unduly lenient for an unprovoked home invasion with weapon use and serious injury.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 following conviction after retrial at Derby Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted; father's sentence increased from four to seven years and son's from two to three and a half years' YOI detention, with ASBO periods reduced from five to three years to reflect double jeopardy.
enrichment.ratio: Aggravated burglary of this gravity, involving a premeditated early-morning attack on a victim in his own home with a weapon, repeated blows to vulnerable areas and serious lasting injury, required at least eight years for the father and four years for the son at first instance; the sentences passed were unduly lenient though reduced on reference to account for double jeopardy.
legal_issues: Whether sentences of four and two years were unduly lenient for aggravated burglary with serious injury
Appropriate uplift for aggravating features including weapon use and home invasion
Effect of youth and parental influence on the son's sentence
Application of double jeopardy principle on an Attorney General's reference

enrichment.short_title: Kidnap-driven emerald theft and Holdup or Robbery Limit exclusion
key_facts: A Sao Paulo jeweller insured under a Lloyd's Jewellers Block Policy lost emeralds after its managing director was kidnapped and forced to remove stock from the premises.
Kidnappers threatened the MD's family elsewhere and used a two-way radio; staff assisted under duress but no violence was threatened to persons at the premises.
Moore-Bick J granted summary judgment on coverage, holding the Holdup or Robbery Limit did not apply; the underwriter appealed on that clause alone.
Special Condition (A) III capped liability for loss by robbery when premises were open or staff present; the Outside Limit clause was accepted inapplicable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Moore-Bick J's summary judgment on construction of a Lloyd's jewellers block policy Holdup or Robbery Limit clause.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the Holdup or Robbery Limit did not apply because the clause addresses violence or threats directed at the assured or employees at the premises, not duress arising from threats to family members elsewhere.
enrichment.ratio: In an ordinary commercial man's reading of the Holdup or Robbery Limit, robbery requires violence or threats against the assured or its employees at the premises when open or attended; loss caused by a director acting under duress from threats to family members off-site, even if stock is removed from the premises, is not loss by robbery within the special condition.
legal_issues: Construction of Holdup or Robbery Limit in Lloyd's NMA 2480 jewellers block policy
Whether kidnapping and off-premises threats constituted robbery at the premises
Distinction between extortion and robbery under English and Brazilian law for insurance purposes
Application of contra proferentem to special conditions restricting all-risks cover

enrichment.short_title: POLO shape mark: limits on amending unregistrable applications
key_facts: Nestle applied to register the three-dimensional shape of a POLO mint without colour or size limitations in Class 30 for sugar confectionery.
Mars opposed; the Hearing Officer held acquired distinctiveness existed only for white mints of standard POLO size and invited amendment via Form TM21.
Nestle sought to limit the specification and add colour and size restrictions under sections 13 and 39(1); Lloyd J held this substantially affected mark identity and refused registration.
The Court of Appeal upheld Lloyd J, requiring a fresh application for the amended mark.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from Lloyd J's decision setting aside the Registrar and refusing Nestle's application to register a shape mark subject to post-filing colour and size limitations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused; Nestle could not use section 13 limitations or section 39(1) goods restrictions to amend an application whose graphic representation lacked essential distinctive elements.
enrichment.ratio: Where acquired distinctiveness exists only for a mark with specified colour and size features absent from the original application, requiring those features is an amendment that substantially affects the identity of the mark and is prohibited by section 39(2); section 13 limits rights conferred by registration and cannot be used to circumvent section 39's restrictive amendment regime.
legal_issues: Whether colour and size requirements are section 13 limitations on rights or amendments to mark identity
Construction of section 39(1) restriction of goods versus restriction of the mark itself
Relationship between sections 13 and 39 of the Trade Marks Act 1994
Whether a fresh application is required when an initially over-broad shape mark is unregistrable without added features

enrichment.short_title: VAT fraud confiscation: lifting corporate veil over company assets
key_facts: Omar, a college lecturer, allowed his company Cambridge Computer Supplies Ltd to be used in a carousel VAT fraud after Skidmore and Withers fell out over Computerwise.
CCSL had traded legitimately before August 1997; properties bought from company profits were registered in Omar's or joint names.
Omar was convicted of cheating the Public Revenue and received an 18-month sentence plus a £790,649 confiscation order with three years' default imprisonment.
The judge lifted the corporate veil, treating benefit and available assets as Omar's; co-defendants' orders raised double-recovery concerns.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave of the single judge against a Crown Court confiscation order under section 71 following conviction for cheating the Public Revenue.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge was entitled to lift the corporate veil, attribute benefit to Omar as alter ego of CCSL, include property values as his available assets, and reject Benjafield unfairness and equal-division arguments.
enrichment.ratio: Where an existing legitimate company is deployed as a vehicle for revenue fraud and the defendant runs it as his alter ego, the corporate veil may be lifted for confiscation purposes; benefit may be attributed personally and pre-fraud company-funded property treated as available assets; Benjafield fairness does not require equal division of benefit among co-defendants or reduction because a co-defendant has fewer assets.
legal_issues: Whether benefit from CCSL's VAT fraud could be attributed to Omar personally
Appropriateness of lifting the corporate veil on confiscation facts
Whether properties purchased before the fraud should be excluded as company assets
Application of Benjafield principles to double recovery and proportional sharing of benefit

R v Dimsey and Allen [2001] Cr App R (S) 497
Re H [1996] 2 All ER 391

enrichment.short_title: Cornish farm inheritance dispute and conditional proprietary estoppel
key_facts: Uncle Percy Uglow assured nephew Richard in 1976 he would inherit Treludick farm if Richard left the family partnership to farm with him.
The partnership failed and in 1984 Richard received a tenancy of most of Treludick plus Red Down land; Percy's 1999 will left the freehold to great-nephew Peter instead.
HHJ Weeks QC dismissed Richard's proprietary estoppel claim for the freehold but upheld his protected agricultural tenancy; Peter abandoned the tenancy appeal.
Richard argued the 1976 assurance was unconditional and his 1976 career change constituted irreversible detrimental reliance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from HHJ Weeks QC's order in possession proceedings dismissing a proprietary estoppel counterclaim over Treludick farm.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on proprietary estoppel; Richard's protected tenancy of 175 acres at Treludick and 25 acres at Red Down stands, with tenancy-related appeals abandoned by consent.
enrichment.ratio: A testamentary assurance linked to entering a farming partnership may be implicitly conditional on the business relationship succeeding; when the partnership collapses and the testator provides a protected tenancy satisfying the equity arising from reliance, it is not unconscionable for him later to leave the freehold to another beneficiary.
legal_issues: Whether Percy Uglow's 1976 assurance of Treludick was unconditional or conditional on the partnership succeeding
Whether Richard suffered sufficient detriment by leaving TR Uglow & Sons in 1976
Whether the 1984 tenancy arrangements satisfied the equity raised by proprietary estoppel
Application of Gillett v Holt and Jennings v Rice to family farming assurances

enrichment.short_title: Permanent school exclusion for cannabis use on school field
key_facts: Pupil M was permanently excluded from CH School for smoking drugs believed to be cannabis on the school field on 3 and 4 July 2003.
Witness statements and a cigarette box containing a spliff supported the school's case; M's second confession admitting use was disputed as coerced by Mr Zweistra.
The Governing Body and Independent Appeal Panel upheld exclusion after rejecting duress and preferring witness evidence implicating M.
M sought judicial review on duress, absence of Mr Zweistra, non-disclosure of prior witness statements, and standard of proof.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an Independent Appeal Panel decision upholding permanent exclusion from school for drugs offences.
enrichment.outcome: Relief refused on all grounds; the Panel lawfully rejected the duress allegation, need not apply the criminal standard from PACE section 76, and ample evidence supported being sure M possessed and smoked cannabis.
enrichment.ratio: School exclusion panels are not bound by PACE section 76; where a pupil's coercion claim is disbelieved, absence of the alleged coercer does not render the process unfair; prior inconsistent pupil statements need not be disclosed where the panel knew witnesses had initially lied and preferred their later admissions against interest; the heightened Dunraven standard is close to being sure and any error would not affect the outcome on the evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the IAP unreasonably rejected M's duress account regarding his confession
Whether Mr Zweistra's non-attendance caused procedural unfairness
Duty to disclose pupils' earlier inconsistent statements to an IAP
Correct standard of proof for exclusion where conduct amounts to a criminal offence
linked_authorities: R v The Headteacher and Independent Appeal Panel of Dunraven School ex parte B [2000] ELR 156

enrichment.short_title: Company headlessee enfranchisement and section 1(1ZB) construction

statutes_considered.title: Leasehold Reform, Housing and Urban Development Act 1993

key_facts: Search Guarantees Plc, headlessee of 51-52 Hans Place with sub-let flats, sought to enfranchise the freehold from Earl Cadogan and Cadogan Estates.
The landlord argued section 1(1ZB) barred enfranchisement because the headlessee was also qualifying tenant of each flat and, as a company, could not satisfy the residency requirement.
The judge declared the appellant not entitled to enfranchise; the appellant contended section 1(1ZB) applies only where the flat tenant and house tenant are different persons.
On appeal the landlord sought to raise a new section 1(1B) 1954 Act business tenancy objection for the first time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from HHJ Levy QC's declaration that a company headlessee could not enfranchise under the Leasehold Reform Act 1967.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; section 1(1ZB) does not apply where the tenant of the house and qualifying tenant of the flats are the same person; new section 1(1B) objection refused on appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Section 1(1ZB) of the 1967 Act resolves conflicts between different tenants in a chain by requiring residency only when a flat forming part of the house is let to a qualifying tenant who is not the tenant of the house; where the headlessee is both house tenant and qualifying tenant of all flats, the residency bar does not apply and a company may enfranchise; a landlord may not raise a new section 1(1B) ground for the first time on appeal without prejudice to the tenant.
legal_issues: Construction of section 1(1ZB) where headlessee is qualifying tenant of sub-let flats
Whether 2002 Act amendments allowing company enfranchisement exclude the appellant

Whether section 1(1B) and the 1954 Act could be raised for the first time on appeal
